records.why: The old analogy said a human cell would be as long as a football pitch and a virus as big as a sesame seed. Both are wrong by a factor of thousands, so students would carry away a false sense of scale. Checked twice: maize grain about 8 mm and a bacterium about 2 micrometres gives 8,000 / 2 = 4,000 times magnification; a human cell of about 20 micrometres x 4,000 = 80,000 micrometres = 8 cm (a palm); influenza virus about 100 nm = 0.1 micrometre x 4,000 = 400 micrometres = 0.4 mm (a speck of dust). A football pitch (100 m) would need a 25 mm cell and a sesame seed (about 3 mm) would be a virus 7 times too large.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e, Chapter 4 (cell size) and Chapter 21 (viruses); CDC influenza virus structure (about 100 nanometres)
records.group_headline: The size-scale analogy was wrong by a huge margin (a human cell is not a football pitch long, a virus is not a sesame seed); it now uses a maize grain, a hand and a speck of dust
records.old: 'If a single grain of dry maize were the size of a typical bacterium, then to match the size of a human cell you would need to walk the entire length of a standard football pitch — such as the ones at Kisumu Boys High School grounds. A virus is so much smaller still that on the same scale it would be a single sesame seed next to that maize grain.'
records.new: 'If a typical bacterium (about 2 micrometres) were magnified until it was the size of a grain of dry maize (about 8 mm), everything would be magnified about 4,000 times. On that scale a human cell would be about as wide as the palm of your hand, and an influenza virus would be a speck of dust less than half a millimetre across, much smaller than a grain of sand.'

records.why: ROOT FIX. A wire mesh or a loose cloth was said to block spores 'physically'; it does not (holes far larger than spores), it only keeps flies off. The same paragraph also stated the three mould species as fact, which no lesson evidences (see group G3). Size check: wire mesh holes are about 1 mm = 1,000 micrometres; spores are 2 to 10 micrometres, so spores are 100 to 500 times smaller than the holes.
records.reference: WHO, 'Five Keys to Safer Food' (keep food at safe temperatures, protect from contamination); USDA FSIS, 'Molds on Food'; mould spore size 2 to 10 micrometres (Madigan et al., Brock Biology of Microorganisms, fungal spores)
records.group_headline: Wire mesh domes and loose cloths do not stop mould spores (the holes are about 100 times wider than a spore); texts now recommend a close-fitting lid, say a mesh dome only keeps flies off, and say covering reduces but does not stop growth
records.old: Covering the sufuria — even with a simple wire mesh dome or a clean cloth, which costs nothing — would have physically blocked the airborne transmission route and dramatically reduced microbial colonisation. Refrigeration would additionally have slowed the germination and growth of any spores that did land, by reducing the temperature below the optimum growth range of most mesophilic fungi and bacteria. The variation in patch colour (white, green, black) across the same food surface reflects colonisation by DIFFERENT species of mould (e.g., Rhizopus, Penicillium, Aspergillus), each arriving via the same airborne route but occupying slightly different microhabitats on the food substrate.
records.new: Covering the sufuria with a close-fitting lid (or a clean upturned plate or bowl, which costs little or nothing) would have reduced the number of airborne spores landing on the food, although it would not stop growth from spores already on it. A wire mesh dome keeps flies off but does not stop spores, because its holes are far larger than a spore. Refrigeration would additionally have slowed the germination and growth of any spores that did land, by reducing the temperature below the optimum growth range of most mesophilic fungi and bacteria. The variation in patch colour (white, green, black) across the same food surface may reflect different mould species (common food moulds include Rhizopus, Penicillium and Aspergillus, but we cannot tell which grew without a microscope) or the same mould at different ages, as white young growth turns coloured when it forms spores; the slimy areas and sour smell point to bacteria or yeast growing alongside the mould.

records.why: ROOT FIX (audit item: confounded design). Old set: A ugali/uncovered/moist/warm, B ugali/covered/moist/cool, C bread/uncovered/moist/warm, D bread/covered/dry/cool, E and F biscuit. New set (checked): A bread moist warm uncovered (baseline); B same but covered (cover only); C same but cool (temperature only); D bread dried (moisture only); E ugali moist warm uncovered (food only); F dry maize biscuit (compare with E: both maize). records.value: (a) The warm, moist samples (A bread and E ugali) showed the most white, green and black fuzzy growth. The cooler bread (C) and the dried bread (D) showed less, and the dry maize biscuit (F) showed little or none. The covered bread (B) still grew some mould because spores were already on the bread, although a lid stops more spores landing. (Mark against what your class's containers actually showed.) (b) The kitchen was warm and the ugali and chapati were moist, so the spores that landed could germinate and grow quickly. Warmth speeds up fungal enzyme activity and growth, and water lets the fungus digest the food and absorb nutrients. The food was uncovered, so more spores could settle on it. All of these conditions were present at the same time, so visible colonies formed by morning. (c) Ugali and the biscuit are both made from maize, but the moist ugali grew mould and the dry biscuit hardly did. So it is the water in the food, not the maize itself, that lets mould grow even when spores and air are present.

value.criterion: Explanation of the phenomenon (what and where from)
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: clearly identifies the patches as living fungal mould colonies, explains airborne spores as the source and route, explains that colour can show different species or different ages of one mould, and notes that slime and sour smell suggest bacteria or yeast.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: identifies the patches as fungal mould and says the spores came from the air, with limited explanation of the colour variation.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: says the patches are germs or dirt, or does not explain how the organisms reached the food.

value.criterion: Use of evidence on growth conditions
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: names warmth, moisture and exposure to air (cover), uses the Lesson 7 comparisons of containers A to F one condition at a time, and links all of them to the overnight spoilage in Kisumu.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: names the conditions and links most of them to the phenomenon, with limited use of the investigation evidence.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: names one condition or gives a vague link to the phenomenon, with no evidence.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: matches each control measure to the route or condition it interrupts, says what it does not do (for example a mesh dome keeps flies off but not spores) and suggests accessible, low-cost options for Kenyan households.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: gives suitable control measures with some explanation of how they work.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: lists measures without explaining why they work.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: accurately describes infections, transmission routes and beneficial and harmful roles, and shows how the same group can be both.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: mostly accurate examples with minor gaps in transmission or the dual role.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: few or inaccurate examples.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: clear, well-organised message for the community that uses accurate scientific terms and local examples.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: clear message with some scientific terms and some local context.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: message is unclear or lacks scientific terms and local context.

records.why: The CBE level 'Below Expectations' cannot be represented: the data contract allows only three level fields (excellent, proficient, developing). Teachers may wish to treat work that does not reach 'Approaches' as Below Expectations when marking. Suggestion: have the partner add a fourth field in a future contract version.

No KICD curriculum PDF covers General Science (the PDFs are Biology, Chemistry, Physics and Mathematics; the Biology PDF has no sub-strand on microorganisms), so the learning outcomes (a to f), content bullets, key inquiry question, competencies, values and PCIs could not be checked against KICD wording, and the 'KICD project requirement' for the mould investigation could not be confirmed. Nothing was changed. All six outcomes are taught (a: Lesson 2, b: Lesson 3, c: Lesson 4, d: Lesson 5, e: Lesson 6, f: Lessons 1, 4, 6 and 8) and assessed in the Final Explanation. Please check the wording against the General Science design if a copy is available.
